title: Growing courgettes
subtitle: From indoor sowing in April to harvest from July through October
excerpt: Courgettes are sown indoors in April and planted out after the last frost in late May. One plant produces more fruit than a family of four can eat at peak season. Regular picking keeps the plant productive through to the first frost.
sourceNotes: RHS courgette growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Joy Larkcom, Grow Your Own Vegetables, public-domain passages. USDA agricultural extension notes on summer squash production, public domain. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), marrow and squash section.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small courgettes that begin to form then yellow, shrivel, and rot at the blossom end before reaching picking size. Usually caused by poor pollination rather than plant disease. The male flowers (on plain stems) appear a week or two before the female flowers (with a tiny embryo fruit behind the petals). If no male flower is open when the female opens, the fruit fails.

content.text: Courgettes are a frost-tender trailing plant that gives a heavy harvest from July to the first autumn frost in the UK. One plant is usually enough for a household; two is a generous amount. Sow indoors in April, plant out in late May after the last frost, and pick regularly to keep the fruits coming. Left unpicked, courgettes swell rapidly into marrows and slow the plant down.

Full sun, sheltered from wind, with deep rich soil or a large container. Courgettes are hungry plants; a planting hole filled with well-rotted manure or compost gives the best results. They need at least 90 cm between plants because of their spreading habit. A 30-litre container with rich compost sustains one plant for the season if kept watered and fed.

Sow one seed per 9 cm pot in mid-April, 2.5 cm deep, with the seed on its side. Germinate at 18 to 20°C. The seedling emerges in five to seven days. Grow on a bright windowsill; harden off for ten days before planting out in late May when all frost risk has passed. Plant at the same depth as the pot; do not bury the stem.

Water deeply once or twice a week rather than a little every day; this encourages roots to go deep and keeps the plant drought-resistant. A mulch of compost around the base retains moisture and suppresses weeds. Feed with a potash-rich liquid feed every two weeks once the plant sets fruit. Keep the area around the stem clear to prevent slug damage.

Pick courgettes at 10 to 20 cm long. Check the plants every two days at peak season; a courgette left three days too long becomes a large marrow. Cut the stem cleanly with a knife rather than twisting. The plant produces flowers and fruits continuously while nights are warm; it stops when night temperatures drop below about 10°C in September. Early in the season, small fruits sometimes abort due to

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main courgette problems and what to do about them.

items.symptom: Small fruits form then rot and fall off
items.cause: Blossom end failure from poor pollination.
items.fix: Hand-pollinate by transferring pollen from a male flower to a female flower with a small paintbrush or by removing a male flower and touching it to the female. This is most useful early in the season before bee numbers build up.

items.cause: Powdery mildew, common on courgettes from August onward.
items.fix: Remove badly affected leaves. Water the roots, not the foliage. The plant usually continues fruiting despite mildew until the first frost.

items.symptom: Plant collapses suddenly in July or August
items.cause: Vine weevil grubs in the pot, or crown rot from waterlogging.
items.fix: Check the root ball for vine weevil grubs (white C-shaped larvae). For crown rot, ensure the planting position or container drains freely. Do not overwater.

items.symptom: Fruit scarred or distorted on the outside
items.cause: Slug feeding on young fruits before they reach picking size.
items.fix: Scatter slug barrier around the plant base. Check under large leaves at night.
